This topic puts the two together: a process with chance in it whose evolution consists of multiplying by the same matrix again and again, and whose long-term fate is an eigenvector.
Un <strong>proceso estocástico</strong>: A stochastic process is a system that evolves in time with an element of chance. And there is a particularly manageable kind, which is also the one that turns up everywhere: the one in which the future depends only on the present, not on how it was reached.
Esa condición se llama <strong>propiedad: That condition is called the Markov property, or “memorylessness”. To predict tomorrow's weather today's is enough; there is no need to know what happened last month. It is a brutal simplification, and yet it works surprisingly well in a great many cases.

What that equality means is the important part: it is the distribution that, on applying one more step of the process, stays the same. The system has reached its long-term regime: there is still movement between states, but the proportions no longer change.
Mira esa ecuación con los ojos del tema: Look at that equation with the eyes of the previous topic: $\vec{\pi}$ is an eigenvector of $P$ with eigenvalue 1. Y de ahí sale una de las aplicaciones má: And out of that comes one of the most profitable applications in history: PageRank. Google modelled the web user as a random walker jumping from link to link. The stationary distribution of that chain says what percentage of the time is spent on each page, and that is exactly the “importance” of the page.
La distribución estacionaria de una cade: The stationary distribution of a Markov chain is, literally, the algorithm that made Google rich. PageRank models a web user jumping at random from link to link, and the importance of each page is the probability of finding them there in the long run: the stationary vector of a gigantic matrix. The same mathematics predicts market shares, hospital bed occupancy and the time a server spends in each state.
Un estado del que ya no se sale ($p_{ii}: A state you never leave ($p_{ii} = 1$) is called absorbing. If the chain has one reachable from everywhere, sooner or later it ends up there, and the interesting questions change: no longer “where will I be in the long run” but “how long will it take me” and “which one will I fall into”.

Andréi Márkov introdujo estas cadenas en: Andrei Markov introduced these chains in 1906 for a surprisingly literary reason: he wanted to prove to another mathematician that the law of large numbers also holds for dependent events. To prove it, he analysed the first 20,000 letters of Pushkin's Eugene Onegin, counting with what probability a vowel follows a consonant. It is, literally, the first statistical model of a text: the great-great-grandfather of today's language models.
Ese tatarabuelo tiene descendencia direc: That great-great-grandfather has direct descendants and can be seen at work. A model that predicts the next letter from the $n$ previous ones is exactly a Markov chain whose state is “the last $n$ letters”: the transition matrix is gigantic, but it is a transition matrix, with its rows adding up to one.
